questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a poster does to its message
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a poster compresses a message for a passer-by.
questions.stem: In a train dispatcher's log, a poster is described as compressing a long notice into one image a commuter can grasp in seconds.

options.text: It strips the message to its most legible element so it can be read at a glance
It repeats the full notice so that commuters can read it at their own pace
options.misconception: believes a poster carries the whole text for slow reading

options.text: It replaces words with numbers so the message can be checked arithmetically
options.misconception: thinks posters work by making a message calculable

options.text: It enlarges the notice to fill the platform so that nobody can miss it
options.misconception: assumes sheer size alone does the work of a poster

questions.explanation: A poster works at speed and at distance, so it keeps one dominant idea and strips away everything that slows reading. Repeating the full text, substituting figures or enlarging it to wall size all defeat that function.
questions.hint: Think about a commuter moving past.

options.misconception: believes street sale means permanent posting

questions.explanation: A penny price, one printed side, a morning date and sale on a street corner all point to a cheap single-sheet publication made for people buying news on the move. Guild notices and private letters do not fit.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Traces of lost-wax casting on a bronze
questions.learningObjective: Explain why every lost-wax casting is unique.
questions.stem: A dispatch log entry mentions a bronze whose wax model was melted out by the molten metal poured into its place.

answer.exemplar: In lost-wax casting a solid wax model of the finished object is encased in a mould, and the mould is heated so the wax melts and runs out, leaving a cavity of exactly the model's shape. Molten bronze is then poured into that cavity and takes its surface from the mould's interior, so every fingerprint, tool mark and surface irregularity of the wax survives in the metal. The mould is broken to release the casting, which means the process cannot be repeated and no two bronzes are identical.

questions.explanation: The wax model is destroyed to make the mould, so the bronze takes its surface directly from the model's shape and no reusable mould survives. That is why every lost-wax casting is unique.
questions.hint: The mould is broken after casting.

questions.stem: A record in the dispatch log notes a carved head where the figure occupies 240 square centimetres of a plaque measuring 30 by 40 centimetres. What percentage of the plaque is carved figure?

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Cracking in a fired clay figure
questions.learningObjective: Identify the likely cause of a crack in a fired clay figure.

stimulus.body: The kiln log for the week reads: the large figure was dried beside a stove for two days, then fired to 1000 degrees over nine hours, and it now shows a long crack running down one side.

questions.stem: Reading the kiln log, a dispatcher identifies the likeliest cause of the crack in the large figure.

options.text: A flaw in a metal armature, which expanded faster than the clay it covered
options.misconception: invents a metal armature inside a clay figure

options.text: A draught in the kiln, which cooled one side of the piece more quickly
options.misconception: blames a draught for a drying and shrinkage failure

options.text: Uneven drying and firing shrinkage, as the outside hardened before the inside
Too much slip in the body, which made the clay run and split as it cooled
options.misconception: confuses a mixture problem with shrinkage

questions.explanation: Clay shrinks as it dries and fires, and if the surface hardens faster than the interior, the outer skin is pulled apart and the piece splits. Drying beside a stove and a long vertical crack are classic signs.
questions.hint: Think about inside versus outside drying.

questions.topic: Joints left open in welded steel
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an open root gap weakens a welded joint.
questions.stem: The dispatch log poses two questions about a welded frame: first, why must the edges to be joined be brought close together; second, what happens if they are not.

options.text: First, the gap allows for expansion; second, expansion closes the gap during heating
options.misconception: confuses welding gaps with thermal expansion allowance

options.text: First, the gap lets the welder see the joint; second, an open gap makes the weld stronger
options.misconception: believes an open gap improves the joint

options.text: First, the edges must be painted; second, paint helps the weld bond to the steel
options.misconception: thinks paint helps a weld bond

options.text: First, the weld needs metal across the whole joint; second, a gap leaves unfused root

questions.explanation: A sound weld needs filler metal to bridge the entire thickness of the joint, so the edges must meet closely. An open root gap leaves un-fused space, so the joint can crack or separate under load.
questions.hint: A weld must fill the whole thickness.

questions.topic: A construction balanced to turn in the air
questions.learningObjective: Explain the condition for a hanging construction to rest in balance.
questions.stem: A dispatcher's sketch of a hanging mobile shows counterweights positioned at different distances from its suspension point.

options.text: Unbalanced, since the heaviest element must always sit directly below the pivot
options.misconception: requires the heaviest piece to hang on the pivot

options.text: Balanced, since each arm turns until the turning moments of the two sides are equal

options.misconception: confuses equal turning moments with equal masses

questions.explanation: A hanging construction turns until the turning moment on one side matches the other, and that is reached by adjusting arm lengths and positions rather than by making every arm or mass identical.
questions.hint: Turning moments, not equal masses.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The audience of a broadside
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a broadside was made for speed and public sale.
questions.stem: A dispatch log entry describes a broadside as a sheet printed in quantity, sold for a penny and dated with the day it appeared.

answer.exemplar: The broadside was made for people who wanted news in public and at once. Printing a whole side on cheap paper let many copies be produced quickly, and selling them for a penny in the street put the sheet into the hands of readers who had not come to a library or a lecture. The date on the sheet marked it as a record of that day's events rather than a lasting text, which is why broadsides were read, quoted and then thrown away.

questions.explanation: Cheap paper, a single printed side, a street price and a day's date mark a sheet made for speed and public sale rather than preservation. It was read on the spot, quoted and discarded.
questions.hint: Price, format and date give it away.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a hanging construction achieves balance.

options.text: First, the arms must be the same length; second, the heaviest mass is placed at the centre
options.misconception: believes balance demands equal arm lengths

options.text: First, the moments on the two sides must match; second, masses are moved along the arms
First, the total mass must be equal on both sides; second, the arms are made shorter
options.misconception: believes equal total mass is what matters

options.misconception: believes the pivot must sit at the centre of gravity

questions.topic: Cracking in a fired clay figure
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a crack follows an applied lump of clay.
questions.stem: A dispatch record notes a clay figure with a crack that follows the edge of an applied lump of clay.

options.text: The lump was made of a different colour of clay, and the colour change cracked it
options.misconception: thinks a colour difference in clay causes cracking

options.text: The kiln was too cold, so the piece froze before the water escaped
options.misconception: confuses drying cracks with damage from a cold kiln

options.text: The join dried at a different rate from the body, so the two pulled apart as they shrank
The figure was fired twice, and the second firing split the applied lump
options.misconception: assumes a second firing explains a join crack

questions.topic: Joints left open in welded steel
questions.learningObjective: Read joint test results as evidence of the effect of root gap.
questions.stem: A dispatch chart lists joint test results: a joint closed tight tested at 100 percent of its rated strength, one with a 1.5 millimetre gap at 62 percent, and one with a 3 millimetre gap at 31 percent.

options.text: The three results show no trend, so each joint differs for unrelated reasons
options.misconception: denies the clear downward trend in the data

options.text: Strength is set by the paint colour of the finished joint and the gap matters little
options.misconception: believes joint strength depends on its finish colour

options.text: Strength falls slightly with gaps, so a 3 millimetre gap still passes inspection
options.misconception: reads a halved strength as an acceptable result

options.text: A wider root gap sharply reduces the joint's strength, so the gap must be closed before welding

questions.explanation: Strength falls from full rating to 62 percent and then 31 percent as the root gap widens, so the gap governs the joint's load-bearing capacity. A joint at a third of its rating could not be signed off.
questions.hint: Read the trend across the three results.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A construction balanced to turn in the air
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a hanging construction settles into a stable attitude.
questions.stem: A dispatch log asks why a hanging construction can settle into a stable attitude instead of swinging forever.

answer.exemplar: A hanging construction settles because gravity acts on every mass and produces a turning moment about the suspension point. Any imbalance between the moments on the two sides produces a rotation, and that rotation shifts the masses until the moments balance. At that point the net turning moment is zero, so the turning forces disappear and the piece comes to rest at an angle that depends on how the masses are placed, not on any fixed level position.

questions.explanation: Every mass generates a turning moment about the pivot, and the construction rotates until the moments on both sides balance. Once they match there is no net turning force, so the piece settles.
questions.hint: It rests where the moments cancel.

options.text: First, it survives inside the finished bronze; second, the bronze is polished to hide the change
options.misconception: believes the wax survives inside the casting

options.text: First, it is melted out by the incoming metal; second, the sculptor refined the wax each time
options.misconception: attributes variation to the sculptor's wax refinements

options.text: First, it is melted out by the incoming metal; second, the mould is destroyed and cannot be reused
First, it is burned out in a closed kiln; second, the metal is cast in separate foundries

questions.explanation: Molten metal melts the wax out through its runners and takes the mould's place, so the wax is gone and the broken mould releases the bronze. With no reusable mould, every casting is unrepeatable.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Joints left open in welded steel
questions.learningObjective: Explain why continuity of metal carries the load in a welded joint.
questions.stem: A dispatch entry asks why a welded joint is described as strong only when the root gap is closed.

answer.exemplar: A weld is not two separate pieces touching but a single continuous piece of metal across the joint, and that continuity depends on molten filler fusing to both parent metals. An open root gap leaves un-fused space running through the thickness of the joint, so the load is carried by a narrow ligament of metal rather than by the full section. Such a joint starts cleanly and then cracks or separates under repeated shock or vibration, which is why inspection insists on a closed, fully penetrated root.

questions.explanation: A sound weld requires fused metal across the whole thickness, and an open root gap leaves un-fused space that the load must cross at a narrow point. The joint then cracks under shock and vibration.
questions.hint: Continuity of metal is what carries load.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A carved head with the block left standing
questions.learningObjective: Explain why relief carving leaves the block's edge standing.
questions.stem: A curator's entry in the dispatch file asks why a relief carving keeps the block's edge visible instead of cutting the figure free.

answer.exemplar: Relief carving treats the block as both material and background, and that shared role decides the shape of the piece. The carver removes the spaces around the figure but leaves the mass of the block standing behind it, so the figure is never truly detached and the silhouette is always read against a solid ground. This keeps the work close to the wall it was designed for, saves the material that a free-standing carving would need, and gives the figure a frame that belongs to the stone rather than being added afterwards.

questions.explanation: The block is both the material and the background, so the figure is never detached and is always read against the standing ground. That shared role saves the material a free-standing carving would need.
questions.hint: The ground is part of the block.

answer.exemplar: A broadside was sold by the sheet to anyone standing in the street, so it had to make sense without prior knowledge or introduction. questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Joints left open in welded steel
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the metal near a weld behaves differently from the parent plate.
questions.stem: A dispatch entry asks what happens to the grain of steel near a finished weld that is not properly cleaned before welding.

answer.exemplar: Steel close to a weld has been heated close to its melting point and then cooled again, and that thermal cycle alters the metal's microstructure over a band around the joint. Paint, rust, oil and moisture trapped against the surface can also be vaporised during welding, and the gases given off can be trapped in the weld metal as pores. The zone right beside the bead therefore behaves differently from the untouched plate, which is why engineers talk about the heat-affected zone and why clean preparation matters.

questions.explanation: The metal near a weld has been heated and cooled, so its structure differs from the untouched plate, and contamination can leave pores in the bead. That is why surfaces must be cleaned before welding.
questions.hint: Heat and contamination both matter.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a poster does to its message
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a poster reads as one strong impression.
questions.stem: A dispatch note asks why a poster is often read as a single strong impression rather than as a set of separate statements.

answer.exemplar: A poster is encountered in passing and for a few seconds, so it must compress an argument into one arrangement that can be taken in at a glance. That is achieved through scale, contrast and position: one element is made large, one is given the strongest colour, and the rest are ordered to support them. A reader who takes in the dominant element and its nearest neighbours has still got the message, whereas a poster that states four things with equal weight leaves the passer-by with nothing to carry away.

questions.explanation: A poster is read in seconds, so scale, contrast and position compress an argument into one arrangement that can be taken in at a glance. Giving four statements equal weight leaves the passer-by with nothing.
questions.hint: Hierarchy makes one impression.

questions.topic: Cracking in a fired clay figure
questions.learningObjective: Identify the choice that most reduced the risk of cracking.

options.misconception: reads leather-hard drying as a hazard rather than a help

options.text: Scoring and slipping the joins, which made the joined body weaker than the rest

options.text: Strength depends on the gap only above 2 millimetres, and is flat below that
options.misconception: invents a threshold below which the gap stops mattering

questions.explanation: The chart's trend runs downward as the gap widens, because the weld can no longer fuse continuously across the section. The joint itself carries the load, so its root quality decides the strength.
questions.hint: Follow the downward trend.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Cracking in a fired clay figure
questions.learningObjective: Explain why hollowing a clay figure raises the risk of cracking.
questions.stem: A dispatch file entry asks why a clay figure that has been hollowed out is especially prone to cracking.

answer.exemplar: Hollowing a clay figure removes the mass that would otherwise shrink evenly, so what remains dries and fires at different rates across a thickness that now varies sharply. The walls at the edges are thin and dry fast, while the thicker core of the body holds water longer and shrinks later, so the two pull against each other. That is why hollow figures are formed with even wall thickness and why the drying is staged slowly rather than hurried.

questions.explanation: Hollowing a figure leaves walls of uneven thickness, so the thin edges dry and shrink sooner than the thicker core and the two pull against each other. Even walls and slow drying reduce that stress.
questions.hint: Uneven wall thickness causes the stress.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The audience of a broadside
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the profit of a broadside run from a pounds and pence account.
questions.stem: A broadside account notes that a printer sold 240 sheets at 2 pence each and spent 3 shillings, which is 36 pence, on paper and press time. What was the profit in pence?
questions.explanation: Sales come to 240 times 2, which is 480 pence; costs are 36 pence, so the profit is 480 minus 36, or 444 pence. The conversion to shillings matters only for keeping the account.
questions.hint: Turn revenue into pence, then subtract.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Traces of lost-wax casting on a bronze
questions.learningObjective: Identify lost-wax casting from surface traces on a finished bronze.

stimulus.body: The record notes the finished bronze: the surface keeps every thumbprint of the original model, a thin line runs from the base to the edge where the metal was poured in, and the patina is darkest inside the folds of the drapery.

questions.stem: From the record, a dispatcher draws the conclusion that the bronze was made by lost-wax casting.

options.text: The pouring channel is a later repair, so the original was made by a different method altogether
options.misconception: dismisses the pouring channel as a repair

options.text: The patina is darkest in the folds, which proves the figure was fired in a kiln rather than cast
options.misconception: reads surface patina as proof of firing

options.text: The preserved thumbprints and the pouring channel show the surface came from a destroyed model
The thumbprints were added by the founder to make the casting look modelled by hand
options.misconception: believes the founder copies finger marks deliberately

questions.explanation: Thumbprints survive because the metal took the mould's interior from the model it replaced, and the pouring channel marks where metal entered and the mould was broken. Patina depth proves nothing about method.
questions.hint: The model left its skin on the metal.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A carved head with the block left standing
questions.learningObjective: State what a relief leaves standing and what the viewer gains.
questions.stem: A closing dispatch test asks two things about a carved relief head: first, what part of the block was left standing; second, what that gives the viewer.

options.text: First, the frame alone was left standing; second, a backing that hides the carving
options.misconception: suggests the carving is hidden

options.text: First, the figure itself was left standing; second, an outline with no modelled form
options.misconception: describes a flat outline rather than a relief

options.text: First, the whole block was removed; second, an entirely free-standing carved head
options.misconception: reverses what remains of the block

options.text: First, the ground behind the figure; second, a solid backing the head is read against

questions.explanation: In relief the ground behind the figure stays standing while surrounding spaces are cut away, and that solid ground is what the head is read against. A flat outline or a removed block would be different operations.
questions.hint: Ask what the head is seen against.
